title: Aged Care Amendment (Movement of Provisionally Allocated Places) Bill 2019
short_title: Aged Care Amendment (Movement of Provisionally Allocated Places) Bill 2019

summary.attribution: Written by a model from the explanatory memorandum; not the record
sentences: The bill would allow the Secretary of the Department of Health to let approved aged care providers move residential care places from one region to another within the same state or territory.

It would amend the Aged Care Act 1997 to permit the Secretary to vary the region to which a provisionally allocated place is attached, after a provider shows the move benefits consumers and meets local need.
The change is needed because the department has been allowing such moves based on a mistaken interpretation of the Act, but the law does not currently support this practice.
changes: The bill gives the Secretary of Health power to approve movement of provisionally allocated residential aged care places between regions.
It aligns the law with the government's existing administrative practice of considering such moves.
It does not allow movement of places between states or territories.
summary.affected: Approved providers of residential aged care and the Department of Health.

speeches.speaker: Ken Wyatt
speeches.brief: The Aged Care Amendment (Movement of Provisionally Allocated Places) Bill 2019 would allow approved providers to move provisionally allocated residential aged care places from one region to another if it benefits consumers and addresses local need, while ensuring places are not transferred from high-need regional areas to lower-need metropolitan areas.

speeches.speaker: Julie Collins
speeches.brief: The speaker supported the Aged Care Amendment Bill 2019, which allows the Department of Health to move provisionally allocated residential aged care places between regions within a state or territory, but not across state borders. The speaker criticised the government for $1.2 billion in aged care cuts under the current Prime Minister when he was Treasurer, resulting in 128,000 older Australians waiting for home care packages and departmental briefings describing aged care funding "losers" tripling.
